title: Canada | Workplace Harassment, Health and Safety and Integrity for Federal Banks
tagline: Prevent harassment and violence, respond the way the Canada Labour Code requires, and live the integrity OSFI expects of every bank employee.
sectors: Federally regulated banks and authorized foreign banks
Bank head offices and operations centres
Bank compliance, integrity and security functions
description:
Banks are federal undertakings, so their staff's health and safety is governed by **Part II of the Canada Labour Code**, enforced by the **Labour Program**, and by the **Work Place Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations (SOR/2020-130)**, in force since 1 January 2021. It also covers the integrity expectations of the **Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI)** in its **Integrity and Security Guideline**, **Corporate Governance Guideline** and **Guideline E-17**.

Paragraph 125(1)(z.161) of the Code requires every employee, including supervisors and managers, to be trained in preventing harassment and violence, and the Regulations require that training within three months of starting, at least every three years and after updates or a move to a riskier role. OSFI expects codes of conduct for all employees to include regular training. All employees should take it; managers, designated recipients, committee members and HR and integrity staff get extra depth.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and good practice; it does not replace your institution's own harassment and violence prevention policy, code of conduct or advice from your HR, health and safety and compliance teams.
audience: All employees of Canadian banks and authorized foreign banks, as induction and periodic harassment and violence prevention training
Managers and supervisors who are often the first to hear about an occurrence
Designated recipients, investigators and HR or employee relations staff who run the resolution process
Members of policy and work place health and safety committees and health and safety representatives
Compliance, integrity, security and HR staff responsible for codes of conduct and background checks
outcomes: Explain why banks fall under Part II of the Canada Labour Code and what the Code means by harassment and violence
Describe the joint work place assessment, prevention policy, emergency procedures, support information and training timetable in SOR/2020-130
Respond correctly to a notice of an occurrence and apply the resolution process, its time limits and its privacy protections
Apply OSFI's expectations on codes of conduct, conflicts of interest, background checks and reporting of undue influence
Keep the right records, meet the 1 March annual report and 24-hour fatality report duties, and explain the Labour Program's enforcement tools

sessions.title: Part II of the Canada Labour Code: why a bank answers to the federal Code
sessions.summary: Why federally regulated banks follow Part II of the Canada Labour Code, what the Code means by harassment and violence, the employer's general and specific duties (including training under paragraphs 125(1)(q) and (z.161)), employees' duties and the health and safety committee structure.
objectives: Explain why banks and authorized foreign banks fall under the federal Canada Labour Code rather than provincial health and safety law
Describe the Code's definition of harassment and violence, including conduct of a sexual nature
List the employer duties in section 125 that drive training, prevention, response and support
Describe employees' own duties and the roles of policy committees, work place committees and health and safety representatives

cards.title: Day one at the Federal Gate
cards.setting: People and Workplace office, Granite Bay Bank head office, Toronto. 8:30 am, Monday.

lines.text: Granite Bay Bank is a fictional federally regulated bank with branches from Halifax to Vancouver. You have just joined its workplace integrity team.
Welcome! I'm Sophie Tremblay. I run workplace health and safety, and our harassment and violence prevention programme sits with me.
Harpreet Gill, branch manager in Surrey. Quick question before we start: my sister works in a hospital and follows the provincial rules. Why don't we?
Because banking is a federal matter. Our people are covered by the Canada Labour Code, and Part II of it is the health and safety part.
Joseph Cardinal, contact centre in Winnipeg. I co-chair the policy health and safety committee. Most staff think health and safety means hard hats.
In a bank it is just as much about how people treat each other. Part II covers harassment and violence too, and it sets training duties for everyone, managers included.
Stage one is the Federal Gate. By the end you should be able to tell Harpreet exactly which rules apply and who has to do what.

cards.title: How a bank lands under the federal Code

scenes.heading: Two levels of law
scenes.narration: Most Canadian workplaces follow provincial health and safety law. Activities that the Constitution gives to Parliament are different, and banking is one of them.

scenes.heading: Banks are federal undertakings
scenes.narration: The Canada Labour Code lists a bank, including an authorized foreign bank, as a federal work, undertaking or business. So bank employees are covered by the federal Code.

scenes.heading: Part II is health and safety
scenes.narration: Part II of the Code deals with occupational health and safety. Its stated purpose is to prevent accidents, harassment and violence, and physical or psychological injuries and illnesses linked to work.

scenes.heading: The Labour Program enforces it
scenes.narration: The Labour Program of Employment and Social Development Canada applies and enforces Part II for federally regulated employers, including banks.

scenes.heading: Regulations add the detail
scenes.narration: Regulations made under Part II fill in the details. For harassment and violence, those are the Work Place Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations, in force since 1 January 2021.

cards.title: The layers you work under
cards.caption: The Act sets the duties, the Regulations say how, and the bank's programme turns them into daily practice.

cards.question: Harpreet manages a branch of a federally regulated bank in British Columbia. Which health and safety law mainly governs her branch's employees?
options: British Columbia's provincial workplace safety law
Part II of the Canada Labour Code
The Bank Act's consumer provisions
Only the bank's internal code of conduct
cards.explanation: Banks, including authorized foreign banks, are federal undertakings under the Canada Labour Code, so Part II governs their employees' health and safety wherever the branch sits. The Bank Act's consumer provisions deal with customers, not workplace safety.

cards.title: What the Code means by harassment and violence
cards.body:
Part II uses one combined term: **harassment and violence**. In plain words, it covers any action, conduct or comment that can reasonably be expected to cause offence, humiliation or other physical or psychological injury or illness to an employee.

- It **expressly includes conduct of a sexual nature**, so sexual harassment is inside the definition.
- It covers words as well as acts: comments, messages and jokes count.
- The test is **objective**: what can reasonably be expected to cause harm, not only what the speaker meant.
- It covers psychological harm, not only physical injury.

Separately, the Canadian Human Rights Act treats harassment in employment on a prohibited ground (such as race, sex, religion, age, disability or sexual orientation) as a discriminatory practice, and deems sexual harassment to be harassment on a prohibited ground. The harassment training must explain how the two connect.

cards.title: Inside or outside the definition?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation: could it be harassment and violence under Part II, or is it ordinary management?

items.text: Repeated jokes about a teller's accent in the staff room
A manager sets clear, achievable sales targets for the team
Unwanted comments about a colleague's body in a team chat
A supervisor gives fair, private feedback on an error
A customer threatens to wait for an employee after closing
Shouting at an analyst in front of the floor and calling them useless
Changing a rota with notice to cover a staff shortage
Sending a colleague unwanted messages after they asked you to stop

cards.title: The training question
cards.setting: Video call between Toronto and Winnipeg, 11:00 am.

lines.text: Our contact centre hired forty people last quarter. Half of them have not done the harassment course yet. Is that a problem or just good practice?
It is a legal duty. Section 125 lists the employer's specific duties, and two of them are about training.
Daniel Osei, HR business partner. One is general: every employee gets the information, instruction, training and supervision they need to be safe at work.
The other is specific: employees, including supervisors and managers, must be trained in preventing harassment and violence and told their rights and obligations.
And the Regulations say when?
They do, and we will get there in stage two. For now, write this down: the employer itself must also be trained, and so must whoever receives complaints.

cards.title: A new manager skips the course
cards.situation: Marco, a newly promoted team leader in Halifax, tells Daniel he will not take the harassment and violence prevention training. 'I'm a manager now. Training is for frontline staff, and I have targets to hit.' His start date as a manager was three weeks ago.

choices.text: Explain that the Code requires training for employees including those with supervisory or managerial roles, and book him into the next session with a firm date
choices.outcome: Right. The Code names supervisors and managers expressly. Daniel records the booking so the bank can show the training happened on time.

choices.text: Let it go because he already took the course as a teller two years ago
choices.outcome: Partly right. His earlier training still counts for the three-year cycle, but a move into a role with new risks can trigger fresh training, and managers need to know how to respond. Check before waiving.

choices.text: Agree that managers are exempt and focus training on his team
choices.outcome: Poor. Managers are not exempt. They are often the first to hear about an occurrence, so the bank would fail its duty and leave the team exposed.

cards.title: Who sits at the health and safety table
cards.caption: Thresholds from sections 134.1, 135 and 136 of the Code. Committees have both employer and employee members.

items.label: Policy health and safety committee
items.left: Employers that normally employ 300 or more employees directly
items.right: Handles health and safety matters across the whole organisation

items.label: Work place health and safety committee
items.left: Each work place with 20 or more employees normally employed
items.right: Handles health and safety matters in that work place

items.label: Health and safety representative
items.left: Each work place with fewer than 20 employees, or with no committee required
items.right: Plays the committee's role in a small work place, such as a small branch

cards.back: The employer must ensure the health and safety at work of every person it employs is protected.
Give each employee the information, instruction, training and supervision needed for their health and safety at work.
Take the prescribed measures to prevent and protect against harassment and violence, respond to occurrences and support affected employees.
Ensure employees, including supervisors and managers, are trained in preventing harassment and violence and informed of their rights and obligations.
The employer itself must undergo harassment and violence prevention training.
Whoever is designated to receive harassment complaints must have relevant knowledge, training and experience, including of the law.

cards.title: Employees have duties too
cards.prompt: Match each situation with the employee duty in section 126 of the Code it reflects.

pairs.left: You notice a broken lock on the cash room door
pairs.right: Report anything likely to be hazardous to health or safety

pairs.left: You see a colleague being threatened by another employee
pairs.right: Report a situation you believe breaches Part II

pairs.left: The committee asks for your view on branch security
pairs.right: Cooperate with the committees or the representative

pairs.left: You trip on a loose cable and sprain your wrist
pairs.right: Report an accident that caused injury

pairs.left: Your manager tells you to follow the lone-closing procedure
pairs.right: Comply with the employer's health and safety instructions

cards.question: Under Part II, which statement about protection from reprisal is accurate?
options: An employer may discipline an employee who reports a hazard if the report turns out to be wrong
Reprisal protection applies only to members of a work place committee
An employer must not penalise or threaten an employee for acting under Part II or seeking its enforcement
Reprisal rules apply only after a Labour Program inspection begins
cards.explanation: Section 147 bars an employer from dismissing, disciplining, penalising or threatening an employee because they acted in line with Part II, gave information about health and safety conditions, or sought enforcement. It is not limited to committee members or to inspections.

cards.title: Real case: the federal regime comes into force (2021)
cards.body:
In December 2020 the Minister of Labour announced that, from **1 January 2021**, federally regulated employers would have to carry out a work place assessment, develop a harassment and violence prevention policy, develop and deliver training, and set up a thorough process for dealing with occurrences.

The same announcement brought in **Part IV of the Code**, a system of administrative monetary penalties. Employers that break the health and safety or labour standards provisions can face a penalty of up to **CAD 250,000** per violation, calculated by the type of violation, the size of the business and previous penalties. Penalties for administrative violations, such as record keeping and reporting, started a year later, on 1 January 2022.

The Labour Program's own overview lists **banks, including authorized foreign banks**, among the industries that must follow Parts II and IV. For Granite Bay, that means harassment prevention is a regulated duty, with an enforcement tool behind it.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: Banks and authorized foreign banks are federal undertakings, so Part II of the Canada Labour Code governs their health and safety.
Harassment and violence covers any action, conduct or comment, including of a sexual nature, that can reasonably be expected to cause offence, humiliation or injury.
Section 125 requires training for every employee (q) and harassment prevention training for employees, supervisors and managers (z.161); the employer and the complaint recipient must be trained too.
Employees must report hazards, injuries and suspected breaches, and cooperate with committees.
Policy committees (300+ employees), work place committees (20+) and representatives (under 20) give employees a voice.

cards.prompt: Think about your own branch, office or team. Who is your work place committee member or health and safety representative, and how would a new joiner find out?

quiz.question: Why do employees of a federally regulated bank in Alberta follow Part II of the Canada Labour Code for health and safety?
options: Alberta's occupational health and safety law does not cover financial services employers at all
Banks are federal undertakings named in the Code, so federal rules apply
OSFI adopted Part II as a prudential guideline for banks
Every employer in Canada follows Part II
quiz.explanation: The Code names banks, including authorized foreign banks, as federal works, undertakings or businesses. Provinces do have their own laws, but those cover provincially regulated employers, not banks.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects the Code's definition of harassment and violence?
options: Only physical assaults that cause a visible injury at work
Only conduct that the person intended to be offensive, as shown by their own statements or messages
Only conduct linked to a ground in the Canadian Human Rights Act
Any action, conduct or comment, sexual ones included, reasonably expected to cause offence or harm
quiz.explanation: The definition is broad and objective: it turns on what can reasonably be expected to cause harm, and it expressly includes conduct of a sexual nature. Intent and a human rights ground are not required.

quiz.question: A contact centre hired 40 people. Which Code provision most directly requires the bank to train them in preventing harassment and violence?
options: Paragraph 125(1)(z.161)
Section 128 on refusing dangerous work
Section 136 on health and safety representatives
Section 147 on reprisals
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 125(1)(z.161) requires the employer to ensure employees, including supervisors and managers, are trained in preventing harassment and violence and informed of their rights and obligations. Section 128 is about refusing dangerous work.

quiz.question: Which duty does paragraph 125(1)(q) place on the employer?
options: Publish annual health and safety statistics for every branch and office on the bank's public website
Appoint a chief compliance officer for workplace safety
Give each employee the information, instruction, training and supervision needed for their safety
Train only employees who work with machinery
quiz.explanation: Paragraph (q) is the general training duty: information, instruction, training and supervision for every employee's health and safety. It is not limited to machinery and does not require a compliance officer.

quiz.question: Granite Bay's Halifax operations centre normally employs 140 people. Which body must the bank set up for that work place?
options: Only a health and safety representative
Only the policy committee, which replaces local bodies
A work place health and safety committee
No body, because offices are low risk
quiz.explanation: Section 135 requires a work place committee for each work place where 20 or more employees are normally employed. A representative is for work places with fewer than 20, and the policy committee does not replace local committees.

quiz.question: Granite Bay normally employs about 6,000 people directly. What does section 134.1 require?
options: A policy health and safety committee for the organisation
A single health and safety representative to cover every branch in the country
A committee only in head office
A committee only if employees request one
quiz.explanation: Employers that normally employ 300 or more employees directly must establish a policy health and safety committee to address matters that apply across the business.

quiz.question: A teller sees a customer push a colleague at the counter. Under section 126, what is the teller expected to do?
options: Wait for the colleague to decide whether to report
Report only if the colleague is injured
Post about it on social media to warn others
Report the occurrence and the hazard to the employer
quiz.explanation: Employees must report things likely to be hazardous and situations they believe breach Part II, and report accidents that cause injury. The duty does not depend on the colleague's choice or on an injury.

quiz.question: A branch manager threatens to cut an employee's hours because she raised a safety concern with the committee. Which provision is engaged?
options: Paragraph 125(1)(z.17) on posting committee names
Section 147, which bars reprisals for acting under Part II
Paragraph 125(1)(z.17), which requires posting committee members' names
Paragraph 125(1)(q) on supervision
quiz.explanation: Section 147 prohibits an employer from penalising or threatening an employee for acting under Part II or giving information about health and safety conditions. Threatening to cut hours is a classic reprisal.

quiz.question: Who must undergo harassment and violence prevention training under section 125?
options: Employees, supervisors, managers and the employer itself
Only frontline employees who deal with customers in branches or by phone
Only managers with five or more direct reports
Only members of the policy committee
quiz.explanation: Paragraph (z.161) covers employees including those with supervisory or managerial duties, and paragraph (z.162) requires the employer itself to undergo the training.

quiz.question: When did the federal harassment and violence prevention regime under Part II come into force?
options: 1 January 2018
30 June 2022
1 January 2021
1 September 2026
quiz.explanation: The Minister of Labour announced that the harassment and violence changes and the Work Place Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations took effect on 1 January 2021.

sessions.title: Preventing harassment and violence: assessment, policy and training under SOR/2020-130
sessions.summary: How the Work Place Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations build prevention: the applicable partner, the joint work place assessment and preventive measures, the policy and its required elements, emergency procedures, support information and the training timetable.
objectives: Explain who the applicable partner is and what happens when the employer and the partner disagree
Describe the joint work place assessment, the risk factors it must consider and the six-month deadline for preventive measures
List the main elements the harassment and violence prevention policy must contain and how often it is reviewed
Apply the training rules: content, within three months of starting, at least every three years and after updates or riskier roles

cards.title: Mapping the risks
cards.setting: Policy committee meeting room, Toronto, with Winnipeg and Surrey on screen. 2:00 pm.

lines.text: Today we redraw our risk map. The Regulations say we cannot do it alone: the employer and the applicable partner do it jointly.
Applicable partner? That sounds like a vendor.
It's us! The policy committee. If there were no policy committee it would be the work place committee, and failing that the health and safety representative.
And if we can't agree on something, the employer's decision wins, but we have to record the decision and the reasons.
My Surrey branch had two aggressive customers this month. Does that count as a workplace risk?
It does. Customers, the layout of the branch, lone closing, even family violence that follows someone to work. All of it goes on the map.

scenes.heading: Work jointly
scenes.narration: Almost every prevention step is done jointly by the employer and the applicable partner: the assessment, the policy, the emergency procedures and the training.

scenes.heading: Assess the work place
scenes.narration: Together they identify the internal and external risk factors that contribute to harassment and violence, then design preventive measures.

scenes.heading: Act within six months
scenes.narration: Within six months of identifying the risk factors, they must develop preventive measures, plan how to roll them out, and implement them.

scenes.heading: Write the policy
scenes.narration: A written prevention policy explains roles, risks, training, the resolution process, privacy, support and emergency procedures, and every employee must be able to see it.

scenes.heading: Train everyone
scenes.narration: Training tailored to the bank's own culture and activities reaches employees, the employer and the designated recipient on a set timetable.

cards.title: The work place assessment cycle
cards.caption: Section 5 also requires a review after certain unresolved occurrences, covered in stage three.

items.label: Identify risk factors
items.detail: Culture, conditions, activities, structure, external factors, data, physical design, psychological safety measures

items.label: Develop preventive measures
items.detail: Measures that reduce risk and do not create new risk

items.label: Plan and implement
items.detail: An implementation plan, delivered within six months of identifying the risks

items.label: Monitor and update
items.detail: Update when risk factors change or a measure stops working

items.label: Review every three years
items.detail: A full joint review at least every three years

cards.question: Who carries out the work place assessment at Granite Bay, which has a policy committee?
options: The HR department alone
The employer and the policy committee, jointly
An external consultant chosen by OSFI
Each branch manager separately
cards.explanation: The Regulations require the employer and the applicable partner to carry out the assessment jointly. Where a policy committee exists, it is the applicable partner. HR may support the work but cannot replace the joint approach.

cards.title: Which risk factors must the assessment consider?
cards.prompt: Sort each item: is it a factor the Regulations tell the assessment to take into account, or not part of the assessment?

items.text: The culture and organisational structure of the work place
Family violence that could reach the work place
Past reports and data about harassment and violence
The physical design of branches and offices
Measures already in place to protect psychological health
The bank's share price over the last quarter
Employees' personal political opinions
The marketing budget for a new credit card

cards.title: What the policy must contain
Match the prevention tool to its rule
cards.prompt: Each tool in the Regulations comes with its own review rule. Match them.

pairs.right: Jointly reviewed every three years and updated when risks or measures change
Reviewed at least every three years and after any change to one of its elements
Reviewed jointly after every time they are put into action
Reviewed at least every three years and after any change to its elements
Developed and implemented within six months of identifying risk factors

cards.title: The forty new hires
cards.setting: Winnipeg contact centre, training room. 9:00 am.

lines.text: So, the forty new hires. When exactly do they need the training?
Within three months of the day they start. Then at least once every three years after that.
And sooner if we update the training, or if someone moves into a role with an increased or specific risk.
Like moving from back office to the collections team, where callers can get abusive?
Exactly that. And our designated recipient must be trained before taking on the role, then every three years.
Half the hires started ten weeks ago. I'm booking them for next week.

cards.title: Generic or tailored?
cards.situation: A vendor offers Daniel a cheap, off-the-shelf 20-minute harassment video used by retailers across North America. It does not mention Granite Bay's policy, its designated recipient, branch risks such as robberies or abusive callers, or the Canadian Human Rights Act. Daniel's budget is tight.

choices.text: Build the course with the policy committee, using the video only as one part, so it covers the policy, the human rights link and how to recognise, prevent and respond in branches
choices.outcome: Best. The Regulations require training developed or identified jointly, specific to the work place's culture, conditions and activities, and covering those three elements.

choices.text: Buy the video as it is because any harassment training meets the duty
choices.outcome: Poor. Generic content misses required elements such as the bank's own policy and the human rights link, and was not jointly chosen.

choices.text: Ask each branch manager to explain the policy informally at a team meeting
choices.outcome: Partly right. Local discussion helps, but it is not jointly developed training, is hard to evidence, and may miss required content.

cards.title: The training clock for one employee
cards.caption: Section 12 of SOR/2020-130. The designated recipient is trained before taking up duties; the employer at least every three years.

items.label: Hired
items.detail: Employment begins; the policy is available from day one

items.label: First training
items.detail: Within three months after the day employment begins

items.label: New risky role
items.detail: After moving into an activity or role with increased or specific risk

items.label: Training updated
items.detail: After the jointly reviewed training is updated

items.label: Refresher
items.detail: At least once every three years after that

cards.title: Training: what must be in it

cards.back: Jointly developed or identified by the employer and the applicable partner.
The culture, conditions and activities of the work place, so a bank's course reflects branches, contact centres and offices.
The elements of the bank's own prevention policy.
How harassment and violence relate to the prohibited grounds of discrimination in the Canadian Human Rights Act.
How to recognise, minimise, prevent and respond to harassment and violence.

cards.front: How often is the content reviewed?
cards.back: At least every three years, and after any change to an element of the training.

cards.question: A back-office analyst hired in March is moved in June to the collections team, which the assessment flags as having a specific risk of abusive callers. She completed training in April. What is the rule?
options: Nothing until her three-year refresher is due
She must be trained again following the move to a role with increased or specific risk
She only needs a briefing from her new manager
She can choose whether to retrain
cards.explanation: Training is required after an assignment to a new activity or role with an increased or specific risk of harassment and violence, regardless of when the last session was. A manager's briefing alone would not meet the duty.

cards.title: Make the support and emergency pieces real
cards.body:
Two smaller duties are easy to forget:

- **Support measures:** the employer must make available information about medical, psychological or other support services in the employee's **geographical area**. A national helpline plus local resources for each city works better than one generic leaflet.
- **Emergency procedures:** jointly developed procedures for occurrences that pose an **immediate danger**, or the threat of one, must be available to all employees and reviewed after each use. For a branch, think lockdown, panic alarms, police contact and who calls whom.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: The applicable partner is the policy committee, else the work place committee, else the health and safety representative; if they cannot agree, the employer decides and records why.
The joint work place assessment looks at internal and external risk factors, and preventive measures must follow within six months.
The prevention policy names the designated recipient, explains the resolution process, privacy and support, is open to all employees and is reviewed at least every three years.
Training is tailored and covers the policy, the human rights link and how to recognise, prevent and respond.
Employees are trained within three months of starting, at least every three years, and after updates or a move to a riskier role.

cards.prompt: Pick one risk factor in your own work place (a lone shift, an abusive caller, a layout with no line of sight). What preventive measure would you suggest to your committee?

quiz.question: Granite Bay has a policy committee and many work place committees. Who is the 'applicable partner' for jointly developing the prevention policy?
options: Each work place committee separately
The Labour Program
The designated recipient
The policy committee
quiz.explanation: The Regulations read 'applicable partner' as the policy committee, or if there is none, the work place committee or the health and safety representative. The designated recipient handles notices, not policy design.

quiz.question: The employer and the policy committee cannot agree on the wording of a preventive measure. What happens?
options: The Labour Program steps in and decides the wording within 30 days of a request
The employer's decision prevails, and it records the decision and its reasons
The committee's view prevails because it represents employees
The measure is dropped until both sides agree
quiz.explanation: Section 2 says the employer's decision prevails when the parties cannot agree on a joint matter, and section 35 requires a record of that decision and the reasons. Nothing sends the dispute to the Labour Program by default.

quiz.question: How long do the employer and partner have to develop and implement preventive measures after identifying the risk factors?
options: 30 days
One year
Six months
Three years
quiz.explanation: Section 9 requires preventive measures, an implementation plan and implementation within six months after the risk factors are identified. Three years is the cycle for reviewing the assessment.

quiz.question: Which of these must the work place assessment take into account?
options: External circumstances, such as family violence, that could lead to harm at work
Each employee's personal credit history and any recent changes in their finances
The bank's quarterly earnings forecasts
Customer satisfaction survey scores
quiz.explanation: Section 8 lists external circumstances such as family violence, alongside culture, conditions, activities, structure, past data, physical design and psychological safety measures. Credit history belongs to background checks, not this assessment.

quiz.question: Which item must appear in the prevention policy?
options: The names of every employee who has given notice of an occurrence in the past three years
Who the designated recipient is and how to give notice of an occurrence
The salary bands of committee members
A list of customers banned from branches
quiz.explanation: The policy must summarise the resolution process, including the designated recipient's name or identity and how a principal party or witness can give notice. Naming people who gave notice would breach privacy.

quiz.question: An employee started on 1 February. By when must she receive the harassment and violence prevention training?
options: Within one year after her start date
Before her first day of work
Within her first probation review
Within three months after her start date
quiz.explanation: Section 12(4) requires training within three months after the day employment begins. The one-year period applied only to people already employed when the Regulations came into force.

quiz.question: Which content element must the training include under section 12?
options: How harassment and violence relate to the Canadian Human Rights Act's prohibited grounds
A summary of the bank's annual financial statements
The bank's anti-money laundering procedures and its suspicious transaction reporting steps for staff
The full text of the Canada Labour Code
quiz.explanation: The training must cover the policy's elements, the link to the prohibited grounds of discrimination in the Canadian Human Rights Act, and how to recognise, minimise, prevent and respond to harassment and violence.

quiz.question: When must the designated recipient receive training?
options: Within three months of taking on the duties, the same deadline that applies to new employees
Only after handling the first notice
Before taking on the duties and at least every three years after that
Once, with no refresher
quiz.explanation: Section 12(5) requires the designated recipient to be trained before assuming their duties and at least once every three years after that. Employees, by contrast, have three months from their start date.

quiz.question: A Calgary branch triggered its robbery emergency procedure last week. What do the Regulations require now?
options: Nothing until the three-year policy review
A new work place assessment for the whole bank
Immediate retraining of all employees nationwide
A joint review and, if needed, update of the emergency procedures
quiz.explanation: Section 11 requires the employer and the applicable partner to review jointly, and update if needed, the emergency procedures after every implementation. A bank-wide reassessment is not automatically required.

quiz.question: What must the employer make available about support measures?
options: Free private health insurance for every employee
Information about support services, such as medical or psychological help, in their area
A trained counsellor available on site in every branch and office during all opening hours
A guaranteed paid leave of a set length after an occurrence
quiz.explanation: Section 13 requires the employer to make available information on support services within employees' geographical area. It does not prescribe on-site counsellors, insurance or a set leave.

sessions.title: Responding to an occurrence: the designated recipient and the resolution process
sessions.summary: What happens after someone gives notice of an occurrence: the designated recipient, notice by a principal party or witness, the seven-day contact, negotiated resolution, conciliation, investigation by a qualified investigator, implementing recommendations, the one-year time limit, monthly updates and privacy.
objectives: Explain who can give notice of an occurrence, to whom, in what form and what it must contain
Describe the steps of the resolution process and the principal party's choices, including ending the process
Apply the time limits: seven-day contact, resolution efforts within 45 days, monthly updates and completion within one year
Protect privacy and avoid reprisal while responding as a manager, witness or designated recipient

cards.title: A notice at the end of the day
cards.setting: Surrey branch, manager's office. 5:40 pm, Thursday.

lines.text: Amira from my lending team just came in. She says a senior adviser keeps making comments about her hijab and sent her a 'joke' image. She's shaking.
Thank you for calling straight away. First: is she safe right now, and is there any immediate danger?
No danger, he's gone home. But she doesn't know if she wants a formal investigation. She just wants it to stop.
Then she is the principal party and she gets choices. She can give notice to you as her employer's representative or to our designated recipient, orally or in writing.
Our designated recipient is the Workplace Resolution Unit. Once they have the notice, a clock starts: they must contact her within seven days.
And what do I do tonight?
Listen, write down what she tells you, keep it confidential, and point her to the policy and support services. Let's walk through the rest together.

cards.title: The resolution process in six scenes

scenes.heading: Notice
scenes.narration: A principal party or a witness gives notice of an occurrence to the employer or the designated recipient, in writing or orally. A witness may stay anonymous.

scenes.heading: Initial review
scenes.narration: The employer or designated recipient reviews every notice. If the notice does not identify the principal party at all, the occurrence is treated as resolved.

scenes.heading: Contact within seven days
scenes.narration: Within seven days the principal party is told the notice was received, how to find the policy, each step of the process, and that they may be represented.

scenes.heading: Negotiated resolution
scenes.narration: Everyone makes every reasonable effort to resolve the occurrence, starting no later than 45 days after notice. If both parties agree, they can also try conciliation with an agreed facilitator.

scenes.heading: Investigation on request
scenes.narration: If it is not resolved, an investigation must be carried out when the principal party asks for one, by a qualified investigator with no conflict of interest.

scenes.heading: Recommendations and close
scenes.narration: The employer and the work place committee or representative jointly decide which recommendations to implement, the employer implements them, and the process closes, normally within one year.

cards.title: Who does what, step by step
cards.caption: Sections 15 to 34 of SOR/2020-130. The principal party may end the process at any time.

items.label: Notice received
items.detail: By employer or designated recipient; oral or written; must include parties if known, date and a detailed description

items.label: Initial review
items.detail: Every notice is reviewed; anonymous principal party means deemed resolved

items.label: Contact principal party
items.detail: Within 7 days: receipt, policy, steps, right to representation

items.label: Contact responding party
items.detail: On first contact: same four points

items.label: Resolve or investigate
items.detail: Negotiated resolution from day 45 at the latest; conciliation if agreed; investigation if requested

items.label: Implement and complete
items.detail: Jointly chosen recommendations implemented; completion within one year

cards.question: Who may give notice of an occurrence under the Regulations?
options: Only the person who experienced it, and only in writing
The principal party or a witness, orally or in writing
Only a supervisor, after interviewing the people involved
Only the work place committee
cards.explanation: Section 15 lets a principal party or a witness give notice, in writing or orally, to the employer or the designated recipient. A witness can even give notice anonymously.

cards.title: Three roles, three sets of rights
cards.body:
The Regulations use precise words for the people involved:

- **Principal party:** the employee (or employer) who is the object of the occurrence. They choose how far the process goes and can **end it at any time** by telling the employer or designated recipient.
- **Responding party:** the person alleged to be responsible. On first contact they must be told they have been named, how to access the policy, each step of the process and that they may be **represented**.
- **Witness:** someone who saw the occurrence or was told about it by a party. A witness can give notice, **anonymously** if they wish; a non-anonymous witness gets confirmation of receipt within seven days.

If the employer itself is the principal or responding party, the notice must go to the **designated recipient**. That is one reason the designated recipient must be trained before taking up the role and must have relevant knowledge and experience.

cards.title: Put Amira's process in order
cards.prompt: Arrange the steps of the resolution process as the Regulations set them out.
steps: Amira gives notice of the occurrence to the designated recipient
The designated recipient conducts an initial review of the notice
Within seven days, Amira is told the notice was received, how to access the policy, the steps and her right to representation
The responding party is contacted and told the same four points
Reasonable efforts to resolve begin, no later than 45 days after notice
An investigation is held because Amira asks for one after resolution efforts fail
Jointly agreed recommendations are implemented and the process is completed

cards.title: Choosing an investigator
cards.setting: Video call, Workplace Resolution Unit, Toronto. Two weeks later.

lines.text: Negotiated resolution didn't work, and Amira has asked for an investigation. The adviser's manager offered to investigate. He knows both of them well.
That is exactly the problem. The investigator must give everyone a written statement that they have no conflict of interest.
We built a list of investigators jointly with the employer last year, so we pick from that list.
Without a list, the parties would need to agree, and if there was no agreement within 60 days we would use someone the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety identifies.
And whoever we use must be trained in investigative techniques and know the Code and the Canadian Human Rights Act.

cards.title: The team wants to know
cards.situation: Three weeks into the investigation, the adviser's colleagues in Surrey ask Harpreet what is going on. One says, 'We heard Amira made a complaint. Is he getting fired? We'd like to know who to trust.' Harpreet wants to calm the team down.

choices.text: Tell the team that a confidential process is under way, that she cannot discuss any individual matter, remind them of the policy and the no-reprisal rule, and offer support information
choices.outcome: Best. The policy must explain how privacy is protected, the investigator's report must not identify people, and committees get no identifying details without consent. Reminding staff about reprisal protects everyone.

choices.text: Confirm that Amira gave notice so the team understands why the adviser is working from another branch
choices.outcome: Poor. This reveals a principal party's identity, exposes her to gossip or retaliation and breaks the confidentiality the policy promises.

choices.text: Say nothing at all and cancel the next team meeting
choices.outcome: Partly right. It protects privacy, but leaving staff without any reminder of the policy, support or reprisal protection can let rumours grow.

cards.title: The numbers that run the process
cards.caption: Sections 20 to 34 of SOR/2020-130 and subsection 125(4) of the Code.

items.label: Contact principal party
items.detail: From notice: confirm receipt, policy, steps, representation

items.label: Start resolving
items.detail: Reasonable efforts must begin no later than this

items.label: Agree an investigator
items.detail: Without a list or agreement, use one identified by CCOHS

items.label: Status updates
items.detail: To principal and responding parties until completion

items.label: Complete the process
items.detail: From notice; longer if a party is absent over 90 days

items.label: Former employees
items.detail: Occurrences known within this period after employment ends are covered

cards.front: Can the principal party stop the process?
cards.back: Yes. They may end it at any time by telling the employer or designated recipient.
No. It must be carried out if the occurrence is not resolved and the principal party asks for one.
No. Both the principal and responding parties must agree to it and to the facilitator.

cards.front: What does the investigator's report contain?
cards.back: A general description, conclusions including workplace factors that contributed, and recommendations, without identifying anyone.
The principal party, the responding party, the work place committee or representative, and the designated recipient if notified.

cards.front: Do committees learn who was involved?
cards.back: No. Under the Code, committees do not receive information likely to reveal identity without the person's consent.

cards.question: The adviser in Amira's case goes on leave for four months shortly after notice was given. How does the one-year time limit change?
options: It does not change
The process must be completed within the later of one year from notice and six months after the adviser returns
The process is suspended indefinitely
The process closes automatically
cards.explanation: If a principal or responding party is absent for more than 90 consecutive days after notice, the process must be completed within the later of one year after notice and six months after that party returns. The process is not suspended or closed.

cards.title: The internal complaint route still exists
cards.body:
Separately from the notice process, section **127.1** of the Code lets an employee who believes Part II has been broken raise a complaint, orally or in writing. For harassment and violence, the employee may go to their **supervisor or to the person named in the prevention policy**, and both sides should try to resolve it quickly.

Unlike other health and safety complaints, an unresolved harassment complaint is **not** sent to the committee for a joint investigation. That keeps identities out of committee hands. Former employees can also complain within the time the Regulations allow.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: A principal party or witness can give notice orally or in writing to the employer or the designated recipient; witnesses may be anonymous.
The principal party must be contacted within seven days and can end the process at any time.
Resolution efforts start within 45 days; conciliation needs both parties' agreement; an investigation follows on request.
Investigators must be qualified, conflict-free and chosen from a joint list, by agreement or via CCOHS; reports do not identify people.
Monthly updates continue until completion, normally within one year of notice.

cards.prompt: If a colleague told you tomorrow about something that happened to them at work, what would you say in the first two minutes, and where would you point them?

quiz.question: A witness wants to report a manager's abusive behaviour towards a teller but fears being identified. What do the Regulations allow?
options: Only the teller may give notice
The witness must sign a written statement
The witness may give notice anonymously
The witness must go to the Labour Program first
quiz.explanation: Section 15(4) lets a witness give notice anonymously. Notice can come from a principal party or a witness and does not have to be signed or sent to the Labour Program first.

quiz.question: Within how many days must the employer or designated recipient contact the principal party after notice?
options: Seven days
Two business days
45 days
30 days
quiz.explanation: Section 20 requires contact within seven days after notice. The 45-day figure is the latest start for resolution efforts.

quiz.question: The principal party tells the designated recipient she no longer wants to continue. What happens?
options: The process must continue to an investigation
She needs the responding party's consent to stop
Only the work place committee can close it
She may end the resolution process at any time
quiz.explanation: Section 18 gives the principal party the right to end the process at any time. If the occurrence was not resolved, the work place assessment may need a review, but the process itself ends.

quiz.question: Negotiated resolution has failed. When must an investigation be carried out?
options: Always, for every notice received
When the principal party requests one
Only when the responding party agrees
Only when the Labour Program orders it
quiz.explanation: Section 25 requires an investigation if the occurrence is not resolved by negotiated resolution or conciliation and the principal party requests it.

quiz.question: Which person is qualified to act as investigator?
options: The responding party's own manager, because they know the team, the people and the history of the dispute well
Any senior employee at vice-president level
The principal party's chosen representative
Someone trained in investigation, experienced in harassment matters, versed in the laws and free of conflict
quiz.explanation: Section 28 sets out the qualifications and section 27 requires a written no-conflict statement. A manager close to the parties raises an obvious conflict.

quiz.question: What must an investigator's report avoid?
options: Making any recommendations
Describing workplace factors that contributed
Revealing, directly or indirectly, the identity of the people involved
Being shared with the principal party
quiz.explanation: Section 30 requires a general description, conclusions and recommendations, but the report must not reveal identities. It is shared with the parties and the committee or representative.

quiz.question: Who decides which investigator recommendations are implemented?
options: The investigator alone, since the report's recommendations are binding on everyone once it is delivered
The employer and the work place committee or representative, jointly
The responding party
The Labour Program
quiz.explanation: Section 31 requires a joint determination by the employer and the work place committee or health and safety representative; the employer must then implement those recommendations.

quiz.question: Notice was given on 10 March. The parties have not been absent. By when must the process normally be complete?
options: Within one year, by 10 March of the following year
Within 90 days
Within six months
Within three years
quiz.explanation: Section 33 requires completion within one year after notice, unless a party is absent for more than 90 consecutive days, which can extend the deadline.

quiz.question: A former employee tells the bank about harassment she suffered, two months after she left. Is the employer's duty engaged?
options: No, because the employer's duties end on the employee's last day of employment, whatever happened
Only if she gives notice in writing
Yes, because it became known within three months after her employment ended
Only if the responding party still works there
quiz.explanation: Subsection 125(4) applies the duties to former employees where the occurrence becomes known to the employer within three months after employment ends, and the period can be extended in some circumstances.

quiz.question: To whom must the employer give monthly status updates during the process?
options: Only the Labour Program
The whole team in which the occurrence happened
Only the work place committee
The principal party and, once contacted, the responding party
quiz.explanation: Section 34 requires monthly updates to the principal party from the month after notice, and to the responding party from the month after first contact, until completion.

sessions.title: Integrity and conduct: OSFI's Integrity and Security Guideline, background checks and governance
sessions.summary: How OSFI's Integrity and Security Guideline expects codes of conduct with regular training for all employees, risk-based background checks, internal and external channels to raise concerns, and prompt reporting of undue influence and foreign interference; and how the Corporate Governance Guideline and Guideline E-17 put the board and senior management at the top.
objectives: Explain the integrity and security outcomes OSFI expects and how they relate to each other
Describe what a bank's code of conduct should cover, including conflicts of interest, and the expectation of regular training
Apply OSFI's expectations on risk-based background checks before hiring, on renewal and off-cycle
Describe the board's role in culture and codes of conduct and how concerns and threats should be raised and reported

cards.title: A gift and a question
cards.setting: Integrity and security office, Toronto. 10:00 am, Wednesday.

lines.text: I'm Lena Kovacs, head of integrity and security. Welcome to the vault. Daniel, you said you had a strange one?
A supplier bidding on our facilities contract sent a procurement analyst two hockey tickets, and the same week offered her cousin a job.
That's a conflict of interest question first, and maybe an undue influence question second. Our code of conduct covers both.
Is the code of conduct a legal thing like the Labour Code, or just HR?
It's how we meet OSFI's Integrity and Security Guideline. OSFI expects codes of conduct that apply to every employee and come with regular training.
Stage four is about integrity: character, culture, governance, compliance and the checks that keep the wrong people out of sensitive roles.

scenes.heading: Who OSFI is
scenes.narration: OSFI is the prudential supervisor of federally regulated financial institutions, including banks and foreign bank branches. Its guidelines set out the sound practices it expects.

scenes.heading: Two outcomes
scenes.narration: The Integrity and Security Guideline, published in January 2024, aims for two outcomes: actions and decisions consistent with laws, regulatory expectations and codes of conduct; and operations, premises, people, technology and data protected against threats.

scenes.heading: Integrity supports security
scenes.narration: OSFI links the two: a lack of integrity can make an institution more vulnerable to physical or electronic threats, including undue influence and foreign interference.

scenes.heading: Risk based
scenes.narration: The guideline applies on a risk basis, in proportion to the institution's ownership, business arrangements, strategy, risk profile and the scope and location of its operations.

scenes.heading: Connected guidelines
scenes.narration: It points to other OSFI guidance: the Corporate Governance Guideline, E-17 on background checks, E-13 on regulatory compliance, E-21 on operational resilience, B-10 on third parties and B-13 on technology and cyber.

cards.title: Integrity principles at a glance
cards.caption: Principles 1 to 4 of OSFI's Integrity and Security Guideline, summarised in our own words.

items.label: 1. Character
items.left: Responsible persons and leaders show good character
items.right: Through their actions, behaviours and decisions

items.label: 2. Culture
items.left: Culture is shaped, evaluated and maintained on purpose

items.label: 3. Governance
items.right: Codes of conduct and conflict of interest policies

items.label: 4. Compliance
items.left: Mechanisms verify compliance in letter and intent
items.right: Channels to raise concerns, such as whistleblowing

cards.question: According to OSFI's Integrity and Security Guideline, to whom should a bank's code of conduct apply?
options: Only senior management and directors
All employees
Only staff in customer-facing roles
Only staff who handle confidential data
cards.explanation: OSFI expects codes of conduct to set behavioural expectations, apply to all employees and include regular training. Senior people face extra scrutiny, but the code is for everyone.

cards.title: What a code of conduct should do
Conflict of interest or not?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation: does it raise a conflict of interest to disclose under the code of conduct, or is it routine?

items.text: A supplier bidding for a contract offers you hockey tickets
You approve a loan for your brother-in-law's company
You own shares in a vendor your team is evaluating
A recruiter is a close friend of a candidate they are scoring
You attend the bank's internal training on the code
You accept a branded pen at a public industry conference
You ask a colleague to second-check a payment as procedure requires
A vendor offers a job to a relative while bidding on your project

lines.text: We're hiring a payments operations lead who will have access to high-value wire systems. The hiring manager says a reference call is enough.
OSFI expects risk-based background checks for employees and contractors: before employment, renewed regularly, and reviewed off-cycle when something changes.
And for higher-risk positions?
At a minimum, criminal record checks and credit checks, on top of identity and background verification. Directors and senior management fall under E-17 as well.
Do the checks stop once they're hired?
No. People change, and so does their access. That's why renewal and off-cycle reviews exist.

cards.title: A rushed contractor
cards.situation: A project manager needs a contract developer to start Monday on a system holding customer data. The staffing agency says its own checks are 'basically done' but cannot share results before Monday. The manager asks Lena to approve access now and check later.

choices.text: Agree a start date only once the agency confirms identity and background checks suited to the role's access, and limit access until then
choices.outcome: Best. OSFI expects contractors to be subject to appropriate, risk-based checks before they start, and security accountability cannot be contracted out to the agency.

choices.text: Approve full access and trust the agency because checks are its responsibility
choices.outcome: Poor. OSFI says accountability for security stays with the bank. Granting sensitive access without confirmed checks ignores the role's risk.

choices.text: Let the developer start on Monday with no system access while checks finish
choices.outcome: Partly right. It limits risk, but make sure the developer gets no access to premises, data or systems the checks are meant to protect until results arrive.

cards.title: Risk-based background checks through a career
cards.caption: Section 4.2.1 of the Integrity and Security Guideline and Guideline E-17, summarised.

items.label: Before employment
items.detail: Identity and background verification; often credentials and references

items.label: Higher-risk roles
items.detail: At minimum, criminal record and credit checks for responsible persons and higher-risk positions

items.label: Regular renewal
items.detail: Checks renewed on a regular basis

items.label: Off-cycle review
items.detail: Triggered by set criteria, such as a move to a more sensitive role

items.label: Directors and senior management
items.detail: Suitability and integrity assessed under a written E-17 policy

cards.title: Who sets the tone?
cards.prompt: Match each governance actor with its role under OSFI's Corporate Governance Guideline and Integrity and Security Guideline.

pairs.right: Responsible for strategy, risk appetite and culture, and approves codes of ethics and conduct
Implements board decisions and directs operations within the risk appetite
Independent of operations, with direct access to the board or its committee
Directors and senior managers whose character and integrity face extra scrutiny
Follows the code of conduct, discloses conflicts and raises concerns

cards.back: Using deception, pressure or power, with malicious intent, to bend decisions or behaviour toward someone's own interests.
Covert, deceptive or threatening activity relating to Canada, for a foreign state or non-state actor, such as manipulating or intimidating people.

cards.front: Who to tell inside the bank
cards.back: Raise it through the bank's internal channels so it can be detected and investigated promptly and confidentially.
OSFI encourages reporting to authorities such as CSIS and the RCMP when there are reasonable grounds to believe an incident happened.
OSFI expects to be informed immediately when the bank makes such a report.
Still documented and inventoried for reporting to senior management.

cards.question: Under the Integrity and Security Guideline, which statement about channels to raise concerns is accurate?
options: Only the board may raise concerns about non-compliance
Internal channels, such as anonymous whistleblowing, should be regularly reviewed and brought to employees' attention, along with external channels
Employees should be told only about internal channels so issues stay in-house
Channels are optional for banks with fewer than 300 employees
cards.explanation: OSFI expects effective internal channels, including anonymous whistleblowing, regularly reviewed and brought to employees' attention, and also expects external channels run by government agencies or law enforcement to be brought to their attention.

cards.title: Integrity and harassment prevention reinforce each other
cards.body:
Integrity and respect come from the same culture. A bank where people fear speaking up about harassment is unlikely to hear about bribery or data misuse either.

- Use the **same speak-up message** across the code of conduct, whistleblowing and harassment training.
- Make **reprisal protection** visible in all three.
- Report **themes** to senior management and the board, so culture can be evaluated, as OSFI expects.

The Bank Act's own whistleblowing duties are covered in a separate FCAC-focused quest; here, focus on the culture that lets every channel work.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: OSFI's Integrity and Security Guideline (January 2024) applies to all federally regulated financial institutions on a risk basis.
Codes of conduct apply to all employees, include regular training, address conflicts of interest and are reviewed and monitored.
Employees and contractors get risk-based background checks before hiring, renewed regularly and reviewed off-cycle; higher-risk roles need at least criminal record and credit checks.
The board is responsible for culture and approves codes of ethics and conduct; E-17 covers suitability and integrity of directors and senior management.
Suspected undue influence or foreign interference is detected, investigated and reported, with OSFI told immediately of reports to authorities.

cards.prompt: Does your current role give you access to anything (systems, data, decisions, suppliers) that someone might try to influence? What would you do if someone offered you a favour linked to it?

quiz.question: What does OSFI's Integrity and Security Guideline expect a bank's code of conduct to include?
options: Regular training for the employees it applies to
A ban on all gifts of any value
Approval of each employee's conduct by OSFI
Separate codes for each branch
quiz.explanation: OSFI expects codes of conduct to set behavioural expectations, apply to all employees and include regular training. It does not require OSFI approval or a blanket ban on gifts.

quiz.question: Which topic does OSFI say codes of conduct should highlight?
options: Maximising quarterly sales
Minimising the bank's tax payments
Avoiding conflicts of interest, such as bribery
Choosing the lowest-cost supplier every time
quiz.explanation: Codes should highlight following the law, avoiding conflicts of interest such as bribery and other improper influence, objectivity, and the security and confidentiality of information.

quiz.question: Under the guideline, when should employees and contractors be subject to background checks?
options: Only once, before the first day of work, because a clean result stays valid for the whole career
Before employment, renewed regularly and reviewed off-cycle on set criteria
Only if a customer complains about them
Only when they are promoted to vice-president
quiz.explanation: Section 4.2.1 expects risk-based checks conducted before employment, renewed on a regular basis and reviewed off-cycle based on certain criteria.

quiz.question: A new treasury dealer will hold a higher-risk position. At a minimum, which checks does OSFI expect in addition to identity and background verification?
options: Social media reviews and personality tests
Medical examinations and drug tests
Checks of family members' employment
Criminal record checks and credit checks
quiz.explanation: For responsible persons and higher-risk positions, OSFI expects at least criminal record checks and financial inquiries (credit checks).

quiz.question: Under OSFI's Corporate Governance Guideline, who approves the bank's codes of ethics and conduct?
options: The board of directors
The chief compliance officer alone
The work place health and safety committee
OSFI's supervisor for the bank
quiz.explanation: The Corporate Governance Guideline lists codes of ethics and conduct among the matters the board approves. The board is also responsible for the bank's culture.

quiz.question: Which guideline sets OSFI's expectations for assessing the suitability and integrity of directors and senior management?
options: Guideline B-13
Guideline E-17
Guideline B-10
The Work Place Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations
quiz.explanation: E-17 covers background checks on directors and senior management, expecting a written policy on assessing their suitability and integrity. B-13 is technology and cyber; B-10 is third parties.

quiz.question: A staffing agency supplies contractors to Granite Bay. Who is accountable for the security risk they bring?
options: The staffing agency alone, because it employs the contractors and ran its own checks on them
OSFI, which licenses the agency
Granite Bay, since accountability for security cannot be contracted out
The contractors themselves
quiz.explanation: OSFI states that accountability for security cannot be contracted out and that third parties should face proportional measures, including assessing their background check processes.

quiz.question: The bank reports suspected foreign interference to the RCMP. What does the guideline expect regarding OSFI?
options: OSFI should be told at the next annual meeting
OSFI must approve the report before it is sent
OSFI should not be told, to protect the investigation
OSFI should be informed immediately of the report
quiz.explanation: Principle 10 encourages reporting to authorities such as CSIS and the RCMP and expects OSFI to be informed immediately of any such communication.

quiz.question: What does OSFI say about 'creative compliance' designed to get around codes of conduct or laws?
options: It is acceptable provided the letter of the law is met, even if the purpose of the rule is defeated
It is inconsistent with upholding the intent of the law and can damage integrity
It is encouraged where it lowers costs
It is a matter only for external auditors
quiz.explanation: OSFI says measures designed to circumvent codes, expectations or laws, such as regulatory arbitrage, do not uphold their intent and can jeopardise the institution's integrity.

quiz.question: Which statement about the Integrity and Security Guideline's scope is accurate?
options: It applies to all federally regulated financial institutions, foreign bank branches included
It applies only to Canada's six largest banks and to their subsidiaries operating outside the country
It applies only to provincially regulated credit unions
It applies only to insurers
quiz.explanation: The guideline applies to all federally regulated financial institutions, including foreign bank and insurance branches, proportionally to their ownership, business, strategy, risk profile and operations.

sessions.title: Records, reporting, enforcement and assessment readiness
sessions.summary: How Granite Bay proves it complies: the health and safety records the Regulations require and how long to keep them, the annual report due by 1 March, the 24-hour fatality report, the Labour Program's monetary penalties and public naming, real enforcement examples, and a recap of who owns what.
objectives: List the harassment and violence records a bank must keep and the ten-year retention period
Explain the annual report due by 1 March and the 24-hour fatality report to the Head of Compliance and Enforcement
Describe the Labour Program's enforcement tools, including penalties of up to CAD 250,000 and public naming
Map roles across the programme, from employees and managers to the designated recipient, committees, senior management and the board

cards.title: The inspector's letter
cards.setting: Sophie's office, Toronto. 9:00 am, Monday in February.

lines.text: A Labour Program official wants to review our harassment and violence prevention programme next month. Let's get the evidence ready.
We have the policy, the assessment and the training records. What else will they ask for?
Every notice and what we did about it, investigation reports, reasons for any missed deadline, and the record of any joint decision where we overruled the committee.
And the annual report. It's due by 1 March. Some employers have been fined for missing it.
Fined? For paperwork?
For paperwork. Their names are published too. Stage five is the Inspector's Table: we show our work.

scenes.heading: Keep the records
scenes.narration: The employer must keep health and safety records: the policy, the assessment and its reviews, notices and actions taken, investigation reports, annual reports and more.

scenes.heading: Ten years
scenes.narration: Most of these records, from the assessment reviews through to fatality reports, must be kept for ten years.

scenes.heading: Report every year
scenes.narration: By 1 March each year, the employer sends the Head of Compliance and Enforcement an annual report on the previous calendar year's occurrences.

scenes.heading: Report a death within 24 hours
scenes.narration: If an occurrence results in an employee's death, the employer must report it within 24 hours of becoming aware of the death.

scenes.heading: Enforcement behind it
scenes.narration: The Labour Program can issue administrative monetary penalties of up to CAD 250,000 per violation, publish the names of employers penalised, and prosecute serious cases.

cards.title: Records the Regulations require

cards.title: Real case: penalties for a missed annual report (2026)
cards.body:
The Labour Program publishes the names of employers that receive administrative monetary penalties under Part IV of the Code.

In **April 2026** its public list showed several federally regulated employers, mostly transport companies in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, each receiving a penalty of **CAD 500** for failing to submit the **Employer's Annual Harassment and Violence Occurrence Report** for reporting year 2024, as section 36 of the Regulations requires. For some, the list noted that the employer had since come into compliance, but the notice of violation was still served because the report was late.

The lesson for a bank is simple: the annual report is not optional, a late filing is itself a violation, and the employer's name can appear on a public government page. Diary the 1 March date, assign an owner and keep proof of submission.

cards.title: A bank on the list
cards.setting: Sophie's office, Toronto. Later that morning.

lines.text: I checked the naming page. It isn't only trucking firms. There's a bank on it.
Under the harassment rules?
No, under Part III, labour standards: rules on notice and planning for a group termination. But it shows the Labour Program treats banks like any other federal employer.
That's the point for our team. Parts II, III and IV all apply to us. If we miss a duty, we can be named.
So the evidence file isn't bureaucracy. It's our reputation.

cards.title: The report that slipped
cards.situation: On 25 February, Joseph discovers that the person who used to prepare the annual harassment and violence occurrence report left in the autumn and nobody took over. Data on last year's notices sits in three branch spreadsheets. Some branches recorded names alongside the numbers.

choices.text: Assign an owner today, consolidate the data from the official notice records, report only the required aggregate figures by 1 March, and fix the handover gap in the programme
choices.outcome: Best. The report is due on or before 1 March; it needs counts, categories and averages, not names. Fixing the ownership gap prevents a repeat.

choices.text: Ask for an extension and file in April once the data is perfect
choices.outcome: Poor. The Regulations set 1 March. A late report can lead to a penalty and public naming, as the 2026 examples show.

choices.text: File by 1 March using the spreadsheets as they are, names included, to be fully transparent
choices.outcome: Partly right on timing, but the report asks for numbers, not identities. Sending names needlessly breaches the privacy the policy promises.

cards.question: A Labour Program official asks why an occurrence took fourteen months to resolve. What record should the bank be able to show?
options: Nothing, because time limits are guidance only
A document setting out the reason for the delay
The full names of the parties for the official's file
A letter from OSFI approving the delay
cards.explanation: Section 35(1)(f) requires a document setting out the reason whenever a time limit in section 33 is not met. Time limits are binding, and the record does not need to expose identities.

cards.title: Real case: a bank named under the Labour Code (2026)
cards.body:
The Labour Program's public naming page lists **Equitable Bank**, Toronto, among employers that received administrative monetary penalties in **March 2026**. The four violations were under **Part III** of the Code (labour standards) and concerned a group termination of employees: not giving the required advance notice to the Head of Compliance and Enforcement, not sharing and posting that notice as required, not giving redundant employees a timely statement of their entitlements, and not setting up a joint planning committee. The penalties were CAD 12,000, 12,000, 2,000 and 12,000, and the list shows them as paid in March 2026.

This case is **not** about harassment. It matters here because it shows that a federally regulated bank is enforced against and publicly named under the same Code, through the same Part IV penalty system, that backs the harassment and violence duties in Part II.

cards.title: Stage five take-aways
items: Keep the policy, assessments, notices and actions, delay reasons, disagreement decisions and reports; most must be kept for ten years.
File the annual occurrence report by 1 March, with numbers rather than names, and report any fatal occurrence within 24 hours.
Part IV penalties can reach CAD 250,000 per violation, and penalised employers are publicly named; banks are within scope.
Employers run the programme, committees act as joint partners, and every employee trains, reports and follows the code of conduct.
OSFI adds integrity expectations: codes of conduct with regular training, background checks and board ownership of culture.
